title: When Does Multi-Agent RL Improve LLM Workflows?
subtitle: Workflow, Scale, and Policy-Sharing Tradeoffs

abstract: Outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) can train every role of a multi-agent LLM workflow. Its benefit is hard to predict because the reward assigns no credit to individual roles and a shared policy trades pooled data against specialization. We ask when this training improves a workflow over its base model and single-agent RL, and what each role learns. We train three workflows (Eval-Opt, Voting, Orch-Workers) with GRPO on math and code at three Qwen3 scales, with one policy for all roles (Shared-Policy, SP) or one per role type (Isolated-Policy, IP). Every workflow gains by adapting to its structure; this does not make a role better than training it alone. Single-agent RL in the same structure matches or beats trained Voting and Orch-Workers, and only Eval-Opt under IP can exceed it. Eval-Opt's evaluator learns when to retry and its generator learns to complete the retried attempts, a joint strategy that a single policy trained alone does not acquire. Under SP, per-output token averaging sets each role's gradient share, a hidden hyperparameter absent from single-agent RL, and the solving roles learn slowly; reweighting it gives SP the speed and peak of IP, and its decline. Under IP, a parallel role, whose instances share one adapter, takes one optimizer step per instance per training step and can drift after the peak as its entropy rises and accuracy declines. Merging those steps delays the decline.
setup: We train three workflows (Voting, Orch-Workers, Eval-Opt) on Math (DAPO-Math-17K) and Code (DeepCoder) with Qwen3 at 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B, under two policy-sharing strategies: one LoRA adapter shared by all roles (Shared-Policy, SP) or one adapter per role type (Isolated-Policy, IP), giving 36 cells, each trained once with GRPO. Solving roles (the voters, the workers and the Eval-Opt generator) write candidate solutions, and a decision role (the aggregator, the synthesizer or the evaluator) sets the final answer; the voters and workers are parallel roles, three instances per episode that run in parallel and share one adapter under IP. Every role receives the episode's outcome reward (the broadcast reward), normalized per problem and role identically under both strategies. Each cell is compared with its base workflow (the base model in every role) and with single-agent RL (SA-RL), both as one response and placed in every role of the untrained workflow. Accuracy is validation pass@1 at the selected peak, the highest-scoring checkpoint at step ≤ 300, and peak differences below about 2 points are treated as ties.

workflows.name: Voting
workflows.one_line: Three generators (the voters) answer independently and an aggregator selects among or combines their answers.

workflows.name: Orch-Workers
workflows.one_line: An orchestrator proposes a plan, three workers write candidate solutions, and a synthesizer writes the final answer.

workflows.name: Eval-Opt
workflows.one_line: A generator answers and an evaluator returns a verdict and critique; any verdict other than correct sends the answer back for revision, up to three generator turns on Math.

findings.title: Which workflows gain, and where the gain comes from.
findings.text: Every workflow gains by adapting to its structure (Figure 1(b)), and each decision role learns the rule its structure needs (Figure 1(a)). Adaptation does not make a role better than training it alone. SA-RL in the same structure matches or beats trained Voting and Orch-Workers, and only Eval-Opt under IP can exceed it (Section 4.1).

findings.title: Why Eval-Opt gains most.
findings.text: Its two roles learn a joint strategy. The evaluator learns when to retry, sending unfinished attempts back, and the generator learns to complete them in later turns (Figure 1(a)). A single policy trained alone does not acquire this strategy. With one response at the same length cap, single-agent RL falls short of Eval-Opt under IP; the same retries close part of the gap, and a longer response can close most of it (Section 4.2).

findings.title: Why a shared policy learns more slowly.
findings.text: IP learns faster and usually peaks higher (Figure 1(c)). Under SP, averaging each output's loss over its own tokens gives a decision role with much shorter outputs well over its uniform share of the gradient, and the solving roles learn slowly (Figure 1(d)). This implicit share is a hyperparameter single-agent RL lacks; reweighting it gives SP the speed and peak of IP, and also its decline (Section 4.3).

findings.title: Why isolated policies decline after their peak.
findings.text: Under IP a parallel role takes one optimizer step per instance per training step, and its adapter can drift after the peak as its entropy rises (Figure 1(c)). Merging those steps delays the decline (Section 4.4).

messages.question: Which Workflows Gain From RL, and Where Does the Gain Come From?
messages.answer: Every workflow gains from end-to-end RL, and the gain is an adaptation to the workflow: each solving role improves at the subtask its structure assigns to it, and each decision role learns the rule its structure needs. This adaptation does not make a role better than training it alone. Graded on their own answers, the solving roles end below single-agent RL, and single-agent RL placed in the same structure matches or beats trained Voting and Orch-Workers. Only Eval-Opt under isolated policies learns to use its structure in a way that single-agent RL placed in that structure does not.
messages.result: RL raises every cell above its base workflow on both tasks and reorders the workflows (Table 1). On Math, Eval-Opt goes from the weakest untrained workflow to the strongest under IP. SA-RL placed in the same structure matches or beats trained Voting and Orch-Workers on both tasks. Only Eval-Opt under IP exceeds it, on Math at every scale and on Code at the two smaller scales (Table 1, same-structure columns; Table 4). The gain decomposes into what the solving role learns and what the structure adds on top of it (Figure 2(a)).

evidence.title: Gain decomposition: only the structural part can exceed SA-RL
evidence.text: The structural gain is the change in what the plurality vote, the synthesizer or the revision loop adds on top of the solving role. In every Math cell the solving role gains less than the single model under SA-RL and ends below it (Figure 2(b)). A workflow's margin over one SA-RL response is thus its structural gain minus that deficit (Table 6). Under IP, Voting's gain is mostly its voters' own, and Eval-Opt has the largest structural gain at every scale, from its revision loop (Section 4.2). A workflow can therefore exceed SA-RL only through what its structure adds.

evidence.title: Solving roles: below SA-RL with or without the broadcast reward
evidence.text: Graded on their own answers, the voters, the workers and the Eval-Opt first attempt all end below SA-RL on Math (Figure 2(b)). First-attempt accuracy is not a standalone measure of the generator, which finishes its first attempt mainly when it is likely correct (Section 4.2). The broadcast reward scores each output by its episode, so wrong and truncated outputs are rewarded inside correct episodes (Table 6). Scoring each voter on its own answer, or training one generator alone on its own answer, still leaves the solving role below SA-RL after the peak (Figure 2(c); settings in Table 17). Voting's margin over SA-RL moves with its voters' deficit under both rewards (Figure 2(d)). The broadcast reward widens the late gap but does not create it. A solving role trained inside a workflow thus ends no better than the same model trained alone.

evidence.title: Decision roles: each learns the rule its structure needs
evidence.text: Each decision role learns the operation its structure needs (Table 2). The Voting aggregator, which receives three answers, scores close to a plurality vote over them. The Eval-Opt evaluator, whose loop recovers almost only unfinished attempts, rejects truncated first attempts (Section 4.2). When the Orch-Workers synthesizer writes only an answer, it returns the workers' most common answer; a copied answer cannot rescue an episode with no correct worker, so its rescues come from its longer outputs.

evidence.title: Code: a smaller deficit, since truncated outputs are rarely rewarded
evidence.text: On Code the solving roles end below SA-RL by a smaller margin than on Math. Their truncated outputs fall almost only on problems no instance solves, so a truncated output is rarely rewarded (Table 9). At a common step cap, isolated and shared policies differ little on Code outside Eval-Opt (Section 4.3).

messages.question: Why Does Eval-Opt Gain Most?
messages.answer: Its two roles learn a joint strategy. The evaluator learns the quality criterion that matters here, whether an attempt finished, and sends truncated attempts back; the generator learns to finish an attempt when it is likely correct and to complete an unfinished one on the next turn, so the loop raises the success rate of the retried attempts above the untrained loop and, at 1.7B, above a single-agent generator given the same retries. A single policy trained alone does not acquire this strategy. With one response at the same cap, single-agent RL falls short of Eval-Opt under isolated policies; given the same retries it closes part of the gap, and a longer response closes most of it at the larger scales.
messages.result: Eval-Opt under IP is the only workflow above both one SA-RL response and SA-RL in its untrained structure at every Math scale (Table 1). Its loop recovers truncated first attempts and almost never loses a correct one (Figure 3), so the gain comes from the added turns.

evidence.title: Role outputs: the evaluator retries truncation, the generator learns when to finish
evidence.text: The evaluator sends back most truncated first attempts (Table 2). The IP generator learns to finish its first attempt mainly when it is likely correct (Figure 7), and its retried attempts succeed far more often than in the untrained loop (Figure 3(b)).

evidence.title: Controls: a fixed retry rule reproduces most of the loop; the generator carries the rest
evidence.text: A fixed rule that retries every truncated attempt stays within noise of the trained evaluator at 1.7B and 4B but not at 0.6B, where the evaluator's text often states the answer (Table 11). Under that rule the IP generator does not fall below the SA-RL generator, clearly outperforms it at 1.7B, though with more turns, and leads the SP generator by about the trained IP minus SP gap. SA-RL gains from the same retries, and one longer SA-RL response closes most of Eval-Opt's lead at the two larger scales (Figure 3(a)).

messages.question: Why Does a Shared Policy Learn More Slowly?
messages.answer: The two strategies differ in whether the roles share one gradient. Under a shared policy the roles' shares are set by an implicit weighting: each output's loss is averaged over its own tokens, so the decision role, with much shorter outputs, takes well over its uniform share, and the solving roles learn slowly. This share is a hyperparameter that single-agent RL does not have. Reweighting the loss by role length gives the shared policy the isolated policies' speed and peak, and with them the decline of Section 4.4. Isolated policies have no share to set, since each role has its own update, and a different problem to watch.
messages.result: IP learns faster than SP in nearly every matched pair and peaks higher in most (Figure 4(a, b); every pair's series in Figure 6). Where IP declines, its lead shrinks or reverses (Table 5, Panel B). On Code, at a common step cap, IP leads clearly only for Eval-Opt at the two smaller scales (Table 8).

evidence.title: Gradients: the decision role holds most of the shared gradient
evidence.text: Under the per-output token mean, the decision role on Math holds well over its uniform share at every probed checkpoint, and about that share or less under an all-token mean (Figure 4(c); Appendix D.2). The slow learning of SP is not due to smaller parameter changes; its adapter moves farther per step than the IP adapters in most pairs (Table 13, Panel D2). On Code the shares stay near uniform.

evidence.title: Role outputs: the SP deficit sits in the solving roles
evidence.text: Early in training the SP solving roles trail in nearly every Math pair (Table 14). At the peak the gap lies in the solving roles for Voting at the two larger scales and in the generator's later turns for Eval-Opt (Section 4.2). In Orch-Workers any lead of the IP workers does not carry over to episode accuracy.

evidence.title: Controls: length reweighting gives SP the IP speed and the IP decline
evidence.text: Scaling each role's loss by its mean output length in Voting-SP-1.7B-Math moves the shared gradient toward the voters. The shared policy then learns almost as fast as the isolated policies, peaks within noise of them and declines (Table 17; Figure 6). Its voters close more than half of their early gap to the isolated voters (Appendix D.2), so the share contributes to the solving roles' slow early learning.

messages.question: Why Do Isolated Policies Decline After Their Peak?
messages.answer: Under isolated policies a parallel role, one whose instances share one adapter, takes one optimizer step per instance in each training step. On Math at the two larger scales this adapter drifts: its parameter changes keep their direction more than noise would, and its outputs grow less stable, with per-token entropy and change between checkpoints already high at the peak and rising, while the decision roles' do not. The decline requires neither the workflow nor the broadcast reward, and it follows the gradient share: a shared policy reweighted toward its solving roles declines too. Merging the instances' steps into one per training step preserves the learning speed and delays the decline.
messages.result: On Math, Voting and Orch-Workers under IP at 1.7B and 4B decline after their selected peak (Figure 5; Table 5). Eval-Opt-IP-1.7B-Math declines late, without a parallel role or a rise in its entropy proxy. Over the same steps Voting-SP-1.7B-Math, Orch-Workers-SP-1.7B-Math and Eval-Opt-SP-1.7B-Math stay at their peak (Figure 6; Appendix C.1), and SA-RL at 1.7B peaks later and ends near its peak (Table 18). The robust declines are confined to isolated policies.

evidence.title: Training metrics: drift and instability are localized in the parallel role
evidence.text: On fixed responses, the parallel role's per-token entropy and change between checkpoints are already high at the peak and rise through the decline, while the decision roles change only in brief jumps. The SP and SA-RL solving roles change far less (Table 12). In the non-declining Orch-Workers-IP-0.6B-Math the workers' entropy also rises, but their change stays small. Training success falls together with validation accuracy, and at 4B the decline begins within the first epoch, so it is not overfitting (Table 16). The parallel role's logged χ², an entropy proxy, rises above its early level in the declining Voting and Orch-Workers runs, so the drift is visible in the training logs (Figure 5). In most declining runs with a parallel role, its adapter's changes also keep their direction more than noise would (Appendix D.3). The instability and the drift are localized in the parallel role.

evidence.title: Role outputs: the lost accuracy comes from the parallel role
evidence.text: In the declining Voting and Orch-Workers runs, fewer problems have a correct voter or worker after the peak, selection losses rise far less than the voters' and workers' accuracy falls, and by the last sampled checkpoint these outputs reach the length cap more often (Table 15). The lost accuracy comes from the parallel role.

evidence.title: Controls: the decline needs neither the workflow nor the broadcast reward
evidence.text: The single-role control, which has no workflow, and the per-voter-reward control both decline, so the decline requires neither the workflow nor the broadcast reward. The shared policy reweighted toward its solving roles also declines, so the decline follows the gradient share. Merging the parallel role's steps into one per training step preserves the learning speed and delays the decline, which does not appear over a validated horizon longer than the reference's (Table 17; Appendix D.4).

takeaway: Every workflow gains by adapting to its structure, but adaptation does not make a role better than training it alone: single-agent RL in the same structure matches or beats trained Voting and Orch-Workers, so it should be the first baseline to run. Only Eval-Opt under isolated policies can exceed it, because its evaluator learns when to retry and its generator learns to complete the retried attempts, so joint training can help where roles respond to each other's outputs across turns. Each policy-sharing strategy carries its own problem to watch: under a shared policy, per-output token averaging sets the solving roles' gradient share, a hyperparameter single-agent RL lacks; under isolated policies, a parallel role can drift after the peak, and merging its optimizer steps delays the decline.
